Imo @metricxyz is one of the most promising things in the DeFi space rn and I was happy to contribute to this research from @schemacap

Here's your TL;DR ↓

Metric = onchain DEX that can compete with Binance on execution despite having much less liquidity.

1) Capital efficiency

Metric processed $1.01B in trading volume with just $7.12M in average liquidity across 12 stock pools in 20 days.

That's ~141x its deposited capital.

2) Liquidity model

Metric uses liquidity bins that follow stock prices, while curators manage trading strategies.

This keeps liquidity near the market price, so LPs don't have to constantly reposition their funds.

3) Metric vs. @Binance

Metric: better execution in 76/87 completed $100K stock sell comparisons (after Binance's standard trading fee)

Binance: better coverage for larger orders

4) Metric vs. @PancakeSwap

For $10K NVDA buys, Metric offered better execution in 70/73 comparisons, which comes out to ~$17 cheaper per order (median).

5) Metric vs. @Uniswap V4

For $100K META trades on @RobinhoodCrypto Chain, Metric's median quoted execution cost was just 4.4 basis points, compared to Uniswap's 93.5.

Next Hyperliquid here?

On the bright side, capital flowing from other sectors + semis to a successful $ANT IPO...

will eventually flow back into semi balance sheets over the long run. Circle of life. but for semis.

If we look at Anthropic's $900.9B of eventual purchase agreements:

- $AVGO + financing partners: $161.2B in Google TPU leases
- Google Cloud: at least $121.3B
- SpaceX: Up to $120.5B (ceiling, can be cut)
- Amazon: at least $110B
- Microsoft: $47.2B-$49.2B
- Nscale:  up to $44.6B
- Lambda: ~$41.3BN ($34.9B can be cut)

With other identifiable counterparty deals such as:

- $MU (undisclosed), but supply agreement
- $RIOT: ~$28B+ $9.1B
- $WULF: ~$19B
- Akami: ~$11.6B (CPU cloud)
- Volta: ~$10B
- OnePWR: ~$3.4B
- $CRWV (undisclosed)
- Everwind (undisclosed)
- Likely $IREN (undisclosed)
- Zerra DC (undisclosed)

Outside the $900.9B, there's another:

- Additional Google TPU capacity: $125B-$150B estimated

- $AMD: over $20B if Anthropic takes the full initial tranche of Helios capacity

I'm actually personally longer term bearish on frontier lab valuations (I like OpenAI more if I had to pick one due to consumer stickiness). But raising a lot from IPO does help raise their counterparty status.

Regardless of how they utilize it, that's a lot of GPUs, TPUs, HBM, optical networking, and compute needed for the next 5+ years.

Now that we're close to 2027 it's a good idea to stress test downside scenarios where you have:

1. Capex cuts past 2028 
2. Stranded Compute / DC Slowdowns 
3. Finance deterioration (base case)
4. 2x+ rate hikes

Working in parallel and see what happens with valuations of AI longs. 

If you see acceleration despite all 4, I'd argue that's an opportunity. 

> Next-gen of photonics is one of the rare segments with an extreme rise in optical content and ASPs that can offset aggregate capex cuts. 

Everyone’s moving into that space, including Elon Musk doing M&A, Marvell, Samsung and others with M&A… and we haven’t seen economic impact on emerging architectures even hit players from Celestial to Ayar + their suppliers yet. 

If we look at a scenario where there's excess GPUs but power constraints:

We might see slowdown in aggregate accelerator/GPU/ASIC procurement, but your optical engines + light sources + switches players see acceleration.

Especially as incentive to replace power inefficient networking... since different (cheap BOM) optical architectures improves GPU utilization or even HBM requirements.  

So value migrates to players more high-beta to architectural shifts. 

If Celestial projections are $500m -> $1B, and we expect -30% aggregate capex cuts, I'd argue we'd still see upward revisions from Celestial over the next 2 years.

But financing with #3 matters a lot as seen with $AAOI dropping off of a $550M, vs. $COHR getting prepayments for capacity expansion from their customers. 

Companies that rely on external foundries might be less sensitive to #3 since they're not as capex intensive. 

On the other hand, companies in sectors have a lot of floating interest like certain Neoclouds, and require further financing might be the most impacted. 

> Legacy and specialty memory is a different cycle that markets conflate with AI capex.

If consumer demand weakens but at the same time, players like Windbond exits DDR2, pricing durability is longer than markets expect. 

> Wafer/substrate procurement such as ABF, SOI, InP are low cost but large downstream destruction if not secured, so we’ll likely see acceleration here as seen with $NVDA earnings call. 

> qualification cycle players within bottlenecks remain very compelling, since first revenue in a large TAM, relative to MC is material to that company. 

If a company is valued at $400m then they get a $200m of orders, it's more asymmetrical to a certain company than a rounding error to a $50B incumbent revenue. 
_

There’s period of times where prices are dislocated from fundamentals from leveraged players getting wiped. I’d argue that time is now. 

I disagree with a lot of the stupid "it's over takes" but I agree it's a good idea to haircut future capex expectations and forward valuations due to financing tightening + macro. 

It's also good idea to see the nuances and stress test downside cases. 

But TLDR: I'd argue next phase of AI infrastructure is going to be increasingly disconnected from aggregate AI capex growth. 

I just personally wrote 4 things I'm using to stress test jointly some of the names I'm looking at, so I'm more comfortable waiting things out... despite seeing hedge funds getting liquidated left and right and overwhelming short positioning. 

I personally see acceleration in more narrow parts of the supply chain, while markets treat the entire AI trade as one.  

We'll see how things play out on longer horizons.

BTC fell 13% in three days.

Everyone has a theory for why: Nvidia, the Fed, the Anthropic IPO, MSCI, the midterms, the Binance hack.

I ranked all 6 by evidence (and two of them don’t hold up):

#1: Leverage, set off by the Nvidia news

Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO on Nov 12, and Nvidia dropped about 10% at the open.

BTC closed that day at $73,974, and three days later it was at $64,120.

What made it so fast was leverage. About $1.3B of leveraged BTC longs got liquidated on Nov 13 and 14, and every forced sale pushed the price a bit lower and knocked out the next batch.

I'm not sure Nvidia was the trigger, but the liquidations line up almost perfectly with the steepest part of the drop.

#2: The Fed is hiking again

The Fed hiked in September for the first time in about three years. Then October inflation came in hotter than expected (+0.4% vs 0.3%), and markets now see about an 85% chance of another hike in December.

When cash pays more, money comes out of risky stuff first. You can see it in the spot BTC ETFs, which had seven straight days of outflows from Nov 5 to 13, about $1.91B in total.

This explains why we're going down, but not why it happened so fast.

#3: Money being pulled out for the Anthropic IPO

Anthropic is raising up to about $64B and lists on Nasdaq this Thursday. Money that size has to come from somewhere, and some of it may be coming out of crypto.

Matt Cole pointed out that BTC did something similar before SpaceX's IPO in June. It fell into the listing, bottomed a few weeks later and then recovered.

The stablecoin drop fits this story too, but honestly it fits the other theories just as well. One past IPO is interesting, but it's not enough to call it proof.

#4: MSCI dropping Strategy from its index

Evidence: low to medium

MSCI is set to remove Strategy (MSTR) from its USA index after Nov 30. Index funds will have to sell MSTR, which makes it harder for Strategy to keep buying bitcoin.

That's a slow drag over time, so it doesn't really explain a 13% drop in three days.

The two theories that don't hold up

• The midterms: Democrats won both the House and Senate on Nov 3.
That's bad news for crypto bills, but BTC actually went up from $76,709 to $80,443 in the two days after.

• The Binance hack: $6.3B was stolen on Oct 29, and a week later BTC was still at $80,443.

There are three dates I'm watching:

• Nov 19: Anthropic lists. If #3 is right, the selling should ease in the weeks after.
• After Nov 30: MSCI's change kicks in.
• Dec 9: the Fed decides on rates.

What would make me more confident is stablecoin supply growing again and ETF flows turning positive.

If the ETFs are still bleeding by the Fed meeting, that points to the Fed, and that one doesn't fix itself on a set date.

I believe the @nvidia board is not acting in the best interest of shareholders nor in a manner consistent with their fiduciary duties. 

What we know is that the board fired Jensen or forced his resignation for violating company policy and/or in response to the accusation of an affair with a spy. 

They did so without careful consideration of the impact on the company, its customers, its shareholders or other stakeholders. 

They rushed to judgment without the benefit of careful due diligence or even with a basic understanding of the facts. 

How do we know this? 

We know this by how quickly Jensen was fired and how little was known at the time of his firing. 

It takes time to convene a board meeting.  There was time, maybe, for one Zoom. 

And this is a decision that should have been made by a board sitting in person and carefully deliberating the facts once they are known.  

And they should have slept on the decision and met again the day after to discuss the facts, the risks and the other implications of their decision. 

The timing and lack of information did not allow for careful board deliberation. 

While boards can fire a CEO for an inappropriate relationship with a subordinate, it should not be an automatic decision. That is why we have boards comprised of humans and not agents. 

A board should consider whether or not such a relationship was consensual or whether it was an abuse of power dynamics. And a board has to consider what the impact of the firing is on all stakeholders. 

If I were in this board, I would not have rushed to judgment based on articles in the media. I would have made sure the board had all of the facts so it could make a careful and informed decision. 

Boards of Delaware companies have a duty of care which means they must make informed, prudent and good faith decisions. This clearly did not happen here. 

What law firm is advising this board?

All the business school curricula need to be rewritten for the 21st century.

Good corporate governance should be defined as founder control, with dual class stock, not board control. The board is just an advisory board. The shareholder vote is a backup in the event of issues, and shareholder sales are the extreme backup.

This should be obvious from the financial performance of founder-led global tech companies vs manager-led incumbents. And also obvious in terms of just how much value these boards typically consume rather than produce.

After all, typical board members aren’t like execs that a CEO can actually assign tasks. Instead, they have power, and often time to scheme amongst themselves, but lack true operating knowledge of the underlying company. The exception is when there are real founders on the board themselves — but those are exceptions.

To be clear, the 20th century MBA-style corporate governance playbook was actually fine for the era of General Mills, General Motors, and General Electric. In that time period, the individual didn’t matter that much. They didn’t have the leverage that computers give them.

But now the Internet has obsolesced all that. So YC, Founders Fund, and a16z are much better business schools than Harvard Business School, which is culturally obsolete because it is technologically obsolete. The world it was implicitly premised on no longer exists.

However, all these intuitions and best practices, the conventions that built billion and trillion dollar companies, have only been informally advocated in blog posts and contracts. To change the defaults, we’ll need to actually write a new curriculum.

Market participants really need to get over their Jensen/NVDA fetish. If the entire AI trade and bull market is truly dependent on one man dolling out billions in dumb loans to neoclouds and the like, then it was bound to collapse regardless. 

If, however, you truly believe that AI is game changing and compute demand will do nothing but grow exponentially over the coming years, then the fate of Jensen and of NVDA as a ticker, doesn’t matter.

Likewise, Broadcom, AMD, SPCX, and custom silicon producers around the world stand ready to fill any void that Jensen’s departure creates, if any.

I think it will become extremely obvious that swarms of AI agents are the future of performance marketing.

AI works particularly well when outcomes are verifiable. And performance marketing is almost the perfect environment for that. You have CPC, CPM, CPA, conversion rates, ROAS, and ultimately the only metric that really matters: how much incremental profit each dollar of ad spend generates.

I’ve worked quite a bit with performance marketing agencies. It’s a very human-intensive business. You hire specialists for each channel, they come up with hypotheses, launch campaigns, test a handful of creatives, adjust targeting and bidding, analyze results, and repeat.

Now imagine a swarm of agents doing this 24/7, across every channel, running thousands or potentially millions of experiments, constantly generating new creatives, exploring audiences, reallocating budgets, and learning from actual outcomes.

It’s basically a giant closed-loop optimization problem with a measurable reward function.

And unlike many agentic applications where success is subjective, here the feedback signal is brutally clear: did the campaign generate more incremental profit than it cost?

The future of performance marketing looks a lot more like autonomous experimentation than traditional agency work.
